---

Understanding the role of motivation in facilitating student engagement in laboratory-based skill education is essential for promoting effective learning and academic achievement. Traditional physical laboratories in science education are widely recognized as experiential learning environments that foster deep conceptual understanding and the development of practical competencies. Students’ attitudes toward laboratory activities significantly influence the effectiveness of skill acquisition and overall learning outcomes.

In response to the global disruptions caused by the COVID-19 pandemic, computer-based virtual laboratories (VLs) have emerged as a viable alternative for science education, enabling continued access to experimental learning under lockdown and remote learning conditions. While VLs offer flexibility and scalability, their widespread adoption remains hindered by limited awareness and familiarity among both educators and students. Moreover, empirical understanding of the motivational dynamics influencing student engagement in virtual laboratory settings remains underdeveloped.

This study investigates the key motivational factors that affect the efficacy of virtual laboratories in teaching laboratory skills and experimental tasks. Data were collected through a mixed-methods approach, utilizing the Intrinsic Motivation Inventory (IMI) to assess intrinsic motivation, self-reported survey items to evaluate extrinsic motivational factors, and a dedicated Teachers’ Perception of Virtual Laboratories (TPVL) scale to capture instructor-level insights. Quantitative data analysis was conducted using independent samples t-tests and automatic linear modeling (LINEAR) to identify significant predictors of motivation and performance.

The findings reveal that animated graphical learning materials within virtual laboratories exert a significantly greater positive influence on students’ intrinsic motivation compared to traditional e-book-style resources. Furthermore, the role of teachers emerges as a critical factor in enhancing student motivation and engagement in virtual experimental tasks. Positive teacher perceptions and active facilitation were correlated with increased student participation and confidence in using VLs. Additionally, the results indicate a positive relationship between the duration and frequency of VL use and improvements in laboratory performance, suggesting that repeated and sustained engagement with virtual experiments reinforces skill development and conceptual understanding.

These findings underscore the importance of integrating motivationally supportive design elements in virtual laboratory platforms and highlight the need for targeted professional development to enhance teachers’ familiarity and confidence in leveraging VLs. The study contributes to the growing literature on technology-enhanced science education by providing evidence-based insights into the motivational mechanisms underpinning effective virtual laboratory instruction.

---
